title: Use casual forms, report ideas, and talk about activities

grammarPoints.title: Build present short forms
grammarPoints.meaning: Short forms are used in casual sentences and inside several constructions. This lesson introduces nonpast affirmative and negative forms; past short forms come in Lesson 9.
grammarPoints.formation: Verbs: dictionary form / negative ない form. る-verbs drop る + ない; う-verbs change final u sound to a + ない (う → わない). する → しない; 来る → 来ない（こない）; ある → ない. い-adjectives omit です; な-adjectives and nouns use だ / じゃない.
notes: いい becomes よくない. Do not add だ after an い-adjective.
For な-adjectives and nouns, だ belongs to the affirmative short form but not the negative: 静かじゃない.
The dictionary form can describe habits or a future action. It is not the ます stem.
Forms inside a polite sentence can still be short: sentence-level register depends on the final predicate.

examples.english: I do not read the newspaper. (Plain style.)
examples.kana: わたしはしんぶんをよまない。

examples.english: This room is quiet. (Plain written style.)

schemas.context: Describe a habitual action in a plain-style diary.
schemas.omission: The topic may be omitted when clear from context; the model states it when shown.
restrictions: Use a dictionary form for affirmative statements and a ない form for negative statements.
Only nonpast short forms are required.

schemas.context: Describe a habitual action in a plain-style diary.
schemas.omission: The topic may be omitted when clear from context; the model states it when shown.
restrictions: Use a dictionary form for affirmative statements and a ない form for negative statements.
Only nonpast short forms are required.

schemas.omission: The topic may be omitted when clear from context; the model states it when shown.
restrictions: Never add だ after an い-adjective.

schemas.omission: The topic may be omitted when clear from context; the model states it when shown.
restrictions: Never add だ after an い-adjective.

schemas.context: Write a complete plain-style statement, retaining だ in the affirmative.
schemas.omission: The topic may be omitted when clear from context; the model states it when shown.
restrictions: Use な-adjective + だ for written affirmative statements and + じゃない for negatives.

schemas.context: Write a complete plain-style statement, retaining だ in the affirmative.
schemas.omission: The topic may be omitted when clear from context; the model states it when shown.
restrictions: Use な-adjective + だ for written affirmative statements and + じゃない for negatives.

schemas.context: Write a complete plain-style statement in a diary.
schemas.omission: The topic may be omitted when clear from context; the model states it when shown.
restrictions: Noun predicates follow the same copula pattern as な-adjectives.

schemas.context: Write a complete plain-style statement in a diary.
schemas.omission: The topic may be omitted when clear from context; the model states it when shown.
restrictions: Noun predicates follow the same copula pattern as な-adjectives.

schemas.instruction: Write only the requested Japanese verb form.
schemas.context: Prepare a short form before putting it inside a sentence.
schemas.english: Form the nonpast negative short form of “{action}”.
schemas.omission: No sentence elements are required in this form drill.
restrictions: Use lexical verb class; 帰る is an う-verb.
Pay attention to する→しない, 来る→来ない（こない）, ある→ない, and う→わない.

grammarPoints.title: Speak casually with close friends
grammarPoints.meaning: Short sentence endings can mark closeness between friends and family. A casual question usually uses rising intonation rather than か.
grammarPoints.formation: Verb or い-adjective short form + ?. With noun/な-adjective questions, use the base without だ. Casual replies can use うん / ううん.
notes: Do not assume it is appropriate to answer a teacher casually just because the teacher uses short forms.
Sentence-final だ is often left out in casual conversation, but retain it before ね or よ.
Particles can sometimes be omitted in casual speech. The model keeps them so the grammatical relationships remain clear.

examples.english: Will you read the letter? (To a close friend.)
Sora is a teacher, you know.
examples.kana: そらさんはせんせいだよ。

schemas.context: Ask a close friend about a future action. Use an ordinary casual question.
schemas.omission: The listener is the understood subject.
restrictions: Use dictionary form with question intonation; do not attach か.

schemas.context: Ask a close friend for their impression. Use a casual question.
schemas.omission: The topic may be omitted when clear from context; the model states it when shown.
restrictions: Omit だ and か in this ordinary casual question.

schemas.context: Give a close friend new information. End with よ.
schemas.omission: The topic may be omitted when clear from context; the model states it when shown.
restrictions: Retain だ before よ for an affirmative noun predicate.

schemas.context: A close friend asks about your plans. Answer casually.
schemas.omission: The speaker is understood.
restrictions: Use casual ううん and a nonpast negative short form.

grammarPoints.title: Express an opinion with と思います
grammarPoints.meaning: Frame a proposition as your thought or belief. The proposition uses short forms even when the final sentence is polite.
grammarPoints.formation: Short-form statement + と + 思います. Keep だ after an affirmative noun or な-adjective inside the quoted thought.
notes: Do not insert です or ます before と in these indirect-thought patterns.
For “I do not think…”, Japanese commonly negates the proposition: …ないと思います.
These exercises use nonpast propositions. Past short forms are not introduced until Lesson 9.

examples.english: I think this game is fun.
examples.japanese: このゲームは楽しいと思います。
examples.kana: このげーむはたのしいとおもいます。

examples.english: I don’t think Sora is a student.
examples.japanese: 空さんは学生じゃないと思います。
examples.kana: そらさんはがくせいじゃないとおもいます。

schemas.context: Politely state your prediction about the person’s next action.
schemas.omission: The topic may be omitted when clear from context; the model states it when shown.
restrictions: The predicted action is nonpast. Use dictionary form inside the polite sentence.

schemas.context: Politely state a negative prediction. Put the negation inside the thought.
schemas.omission: The topic may be omitted when clear from context; the model states it when shown.
restrictions: Keep 思います affirmative and negate the proposition in the target pattern.

schemas.context: Politely express your impression.
schemas.omission: The topic may be omitted when clear from context; the model states it when shown.
restrictions: い-adjectives take neither だ nor です before と.

schemas.context: Politely express your impression.
schemas.omission: The topic may be omitted when clear from context; the model states it when shown.
restrictions: Retain affirmative だ before と for a な-adjective.

schemas.context: Politely express an uncertain belief about someone’s role.
schemas.omission: The topic may be omitted when clear from context; the model states it when shown.
restrictions: An affirmative noun predicate requires だ before と.

grammarPoints.title: Report what someone said
grammarPoints.meaning: Use a short-form proposition followed by と言っていました to pass on something you heard someone say.
grammarPoints.formation: Speaker は + short-form proposition + と言っていました.
notes: Keep the tense of the original statement; Japanese does not automatically shift nonpast to past because the reporting verb is past.
An affirmative noun or な-adjective retains だ before と.
と言っていました suits something you heard being said. と言いました can report a saying without that firsthand-hearing context.

examples.english: Yuna said she would drink tea tomorrow.
examples.japanese: 優奈さんは明日お茶を飲むと言っていました。
examples.kana: ゆうなさんはあしたおちゃをのむといっていました。

schemas.context: Earlier today you heard the person explain their plan for tomorrow. Report it politely.
schemas.japanese: {person}は明日、{object}を{action}と言っていました。
schemas.kana: {person}はあした、{object}を{action}といっていました。
schemas.omission: The topic may be omitted when clear from context; the model states it when shown.
restrictions: Preserve the original plan’s nonpast tense inside the quotation.
Do not use a past short form to imitate English tense backshift.

schemas.context: Earlier today you heard the person explain their plan for tomorrow. Report it politely.
schemas.japanese: {person}は明日、{object}を{action:negative}と言っていました。
schemas.kana: {person}はあした、{object}を{action:negative}といっていました。
schemas.omission: The topic may be omitted when clear from context; the model states it when shown.
restrictions: Preserve the original plan’s nonpast tense inside the quotation.
Do not use a past short form to imitate English tense backshift.

schemas.context: You heard this person describe their current occupation earlier today. Report it politely.
schemas.omission: The topic may be omitted when clear from context; the model states it when shown.
restrictions: The reported noun predicate requires だ.
The current role remains nonpast inside the past report.

grammarPoints.title: Ask someone not to do something
grammarPoints.meaning: Request that the listener refrain from an action. This is generally less forceful than announcing a prohibition with てはいけません.
grammarPoints.formation: Nonpast negative short form ending in ない + でください.
notes: Do not replace this with a verb te-form plus ください; the negative ない remains.
Use this for a personal request or a polite refusal of permission, not for a prediction about what will happen.
The requested action must be under the listener’s control.

examples.english: Please do not close the window.
examples.japanese: 窓を閉めないでください。
examples.kana: まどをしめないでください。

schemas.context: Make a polite personal request to someone who can choose whether to do the action.
schemas.omission: The listener is understood.
restrictions: Retain the verb’s negative short form before でください.
Match the object to the verb.

schemas.instruction: Write a polite reply in Japanese.
schemas.context: A visitor has asked permission to {action} {object}. Politely ask them not to.
schemas.omission: The visitor is understood.
restrictions: Use the personal negative request rather than the stronger rule expression てはいけません.

grammarPoints.title: Talk about liking an activity or being skilled at it
grammarPoints.meaning: Turn an activity into a noun-like phrase with の, then say whether someone likes it or is good at it.
grammarPoints.formation: Verb phrase ending in dictionary form + のが + 好き / きらい / 上手 / 下手 + です.
notes: Keep particles inside the activity phrase: 本を読むのが好きです. The の is required after a verb.
Do not use a te-form just because English uses an “-ing” word.
上手 often praises another person. For your own abilities, 得意 / 苦手 can sound more appropriate.
A する activity can also be expressed with its noun: 日本語の勉強が好きです, alongside 日本語を勉強するのが好きです.

examples.japanese: 手紙を読むのが好きです。
examples.kana: てがみをよむのがすきです。

examples.english: Kai is good at playing the piano.
examples.japanese: 海さんはピアノを弾くのが上手です。
examples.kana: かいさんはぴあのをひくのがじょうずです。

schemas.context: Politely describe how you feel about doing an activity.
schemas.omission: The speaker is understood.
restrictions: The activity ends in dictionary form before nominalizing の.
Match the verb and object; do not replace の with a te-form.

schemas.context: Describe another person’s musical ability using polite speech.
schemas.omission: The topic may be omitted when clear from context; the model states it when shown.
restrictions: 弾く is used for string or keyboard instruments here. Do not insert a flute or drums.
The skill refers to an activity, so retain の after 弾く.

grammarPoints.title: Use が to identify the subject
grammarPoints.meaning: が can mark the new or focused answer to “who?” or “which one?”. は usually presents an already established topic.
grammarPoints.formation: Question word + が + predicate; the focused answer also uses が.
notes: A subject question word is not followed by は.
The choice depends on the conversation. A name does not always require が or always require は.
Keep ordinary を and other particles on the rest of the sentence.

examples.japanese: だれがドアを開けましたか。
examples.kana: だれがどあをあけましたか。

examples.japanese: 優奈さんがドアを開けました。
examples.kana: ゆうなさんがどあをあけました。

schemas.context: You know an action happened but do not know who did it. Ask politely.
schemas.omission: Keep だれ because identifying the subject is the purpose of the question.
restrictions: The unknown subject だれ takes が, not は.

schemas.context: Someone asks who {action:politePast} {object}. Identify the person in a complete polite sentence.
schemas.omission: State the subject because it is the requested new information.
restrictions: The name is the newly identified subject, so use が.

grammarPoints.title: Say “something” or “nothing”
grammarPoints.meaning: 何か means something in statements and anything in questions. 何も combines with a negative predicate to mean nothing or not anything.
grammarPoints.formation: 何か + affirmative predicate / question; 何も + negative predicate.
notes: Where を, が, or は would otherwise appear, 何か / 何も often stand alone. These models omit を.
Do not combine 何も with an affirmative predicate to express “nothing”.
Other particles with indefinite words are developed in Lesson 10; keep these patterns simple.

examples.kana: けさ、なにかのみました。

examples.english: I did not eat anything yesterday.
examples.japanese: 昨日、何も食べませんでした。
examples.kana: きのう、なにもたべませんでした。

schemas.context: Report what happened using polite speech without naming the food or drink.
schemas.omission: The speaker is understood; を is omitted after 何か.
restrictions: Use a transitive consumption verb for which an unspecified object is natural.
Do not add an object noun after 何か.

schemas.context: Ask politely whether someone ate or drank anything.
schemas.omission: The listener is understood; を is omitted after 何か.
restrictions: Use 何か in a positive information question.

schemas.context: Report that no eating or drinking of the specified kind happened. Use polite speech.
schemas.omission: The speaker is understood.
restrictions: 何も requires a negative verb.
No additional を is used in this pattern.

grammarPoints.title: Use early/late to modify an action
grammarPoints.meaning: 早い and 遅い describe nouns or act as adjective predicates. 早く and 遅く describe how early or late an action happens.
grammarPoints.formation: 早く / 遅く + verb. For an adjective predicate, use 早いです / 遅いです.
notes: Use the adverb directly before the verb phrase, not an adjective with です.
This lesson introduces these particular adverbs; the exercise does not assume a general adjective-to-adverb curriculum.

examples.kana: きのう、はやくおきました。

schemas.context: Politely describe the timing of a daily routine.
schemas.omission: The speaker is understood.
restrictions: Use the lexical adverbs 早く / 遅く, not 早い / 遅い before the verb.

grammarPoints.title: Recognize the noun inside a する activity
grammarPoints.meaning: Many する activities have a related noun. That noun can be used directly with が好きです; the full verb instead needs nominalizing の.
grammarPoints.formation: Activity noun + が好きです; activity noun + するのが好きです. With a noun modifier use の, while the corresponding verb phrase may use を.
notes: Do not insert の after an activity noun just because the full する verb requires it.
Only verified する nouns are used here; do not attach する to every noun.
For example, 日本語の勉強 and 日本語を勉強する describe the same subject through different structures.

examples.japanese: 掃除するのが好きです。
examples.kana: そうじするのがすきです。

schemas.context: Express a preference politely using the activity noun itself.
schemas.omission: The speaker is understood.
restrictions: These entries are established activity nouns. Do not add nominalizing の after them.

schemas.context: Express a preference politely using the full する verb and nominalizing の.
schemas.omission: The speaker is understood.
restrictions: The activity noun must be a verified する compound. The full verb requires の before が.

negative.kana: かいしゃいんじゃない
